title: Iora Health: capitated, Medicare-focused primary care model
questions: What was Iora Health's care model?
How did Iora Health get paid?
Was Iora Health in Medicare Advantage or Direct Contracting?
How many patients did Iora Health have before One Medical bought it?
summary: Iora Health was a Boston-based primary care organization founded in 2011 by Rushika Fernandopulle that focused on older adults and took financial risk for their care. Rather than billing visit by visit, Iora contracted with Medicare Advantage insurers (Healthcare Dive named UnitedHealthcare, Cigna and Humana) and, from April 2021, with CMS through the Direct Contracting model, under which payment is tied to the spending and quality outcomes of attributed traditional Medicare beneficiaries. Roughly 60% of its members were in Medicare Advantage in 2021. After the acquisition, One Medical's filings describe this book as "At-Risk" business: Medicare revenue is mostly capitated payments from MA plans and CMS, and the company is responsible for managing the medical costs of attributed members, which shows up as medical claims expense. Scale was modest relative to its valuation: about 38,000 members in Q1 2021 and roughly 39,000 patients (31,000 at-risk) at the end of July 2021, with projected 2021 revenue near $300 million.

facts.payment_model: capitated / full-risk arrangements with MA plans and CMS (Direct Contracting)

title: One Medical's 2021 acquisition of Iora Health
questions: How much did One Medical pay for Iora Health?
When did the One Medical–Iora deal close?
Why did One Medical buy Iora?
Was the Iora deal $2.1 billion or $1.4 billion?
summary: One Medical (legal name 1Life Healthcare) announced an all-stock agreement to buy Iora Health on June 7, 2021. The headline value of about $2.1 billion was based on One Medical's June 4, 2021 share price, with Iora holders receiving about 56.1 million One Medical shares (roughly 26.75% of the combined company). The deal closed September 1, 2021, and Iora became a wholly owned subsidiary. Because the consideration was stock and One Medical's share price fell between signing and closing, the company's 2021 10-K records aggregate purchase consideration of about $1.4 billion. The strategic logic was to add full-risk Medicare capabilities to One Medical's commercial, employer-sponsored membership model; the companies projected about $350 million of annual revenue synergies by 2025. Fernandopulle became One Medical's chief innovation officer.

title: One Medical at-risk (Medicare) segment scale, 2021–2022
questions: How big was One Medical's Medicare at-risk business?
How much of One Medical revenue was capitated?
How many at-risk members did One Medical have before Amazon bought it?
summary: After absorbing Iora, One Medical reported two membership groups: Consumer and Enterprise (commercial members, many paid for by employers) and At-Risk (Medicare patients in capitated arrangements). At-risk membership was small in headcount but large in revenue. At year-end 2021 One Medical had about 736,000 total members, of whom about 33,000 were at-risk, working with eight Medicare Advantage payers across ten geographies, and 182 offices in 25 markets. Capitated revenue was $126.6 million in 2021 (a partial year of Iora). In 2022 the at-risk book grew to about 40,000 members out of 836,000 total, yet capitated revenue reached $517.4 million of $1.046 billion total net revenue, with $419.7 million of medical claims expense and a net loss of $397.8 million. Roughly 5% of members therefore generated about half of revenue, illustrating how capitation concentrates revenue (and medical cost risk) in a small senior population.

summary: Amazon agreed on July 21, 2022 to buy One Medical for $18 per share in cash, a 43% premium to the prior close, for a transaction valued at about $3.9 billion including One Medical's net debt. The deal closed on February 22, 2023, after the Federal Trade Commission declined to sue to block it while saying it would keep examining competition and health-data concerns. Because One Medical had already acquired Iora Health, the purchase brought Amazon a capitated Medicare primary care business alongside One Medical's membership-based commercial clinics. Analysts quoted at signing flagged the Medicare segment as cash-consuming and riskier than the commercial model. At closing, reports described roughly 815,000 members and about 200 offices; One Medical membership remained separate from Amazon Prime at that time.

summary: Evolent, founded in 2011 by management together with UPMC and The Advisory Board Company, now positions itself around specialty care for people with complex conditions, chiefly oncology, cardiology and musculoskeletal care, supported by management of diagnostics such as radiology and genetic testing. Its customers are health plans and other risk-bearing entities; its users are the physicians whose specialty referrals and treatment choices it influences through clinical pathways, prior authorization and analytics. Revenue falls into three buckets in its filings: the Specialty Technology and Services Suite (non-capitated, low per-member fees across a large covered population), the Performance Suite (capitated arrangements where Evolent takes on the medical cost within a defined specialty scope), and Administrative Services (platform and operations contracts). Named customers in its 2024 10-K include Humana, Molina Healthcare, Florida Blue Medicare and Cook County Health. In 2025 it sold its primary care ACO business to concentrate on specialty.

title: Evolent Performance Suite: specialty capitation economics
questions: How does Evolent take risk in oncology?
What is a specialty capitation arrangement?
How many lives are in Evolent's Performance Suite?

summary: In Evolent's Performance Suite, a health plan pays Evolent a fixed per-member-per-month fee and Evolent becomes financially responsible for the cost of a defined slice of care, such as oncology or cardiology services, rather than the member's total cost. Contracts range from gain-share with upside and downside to taking substantially all costs in scope, and may include risk corridors, stop-loss limits and protections for change events; some also put part of the fee at risk on service levels. The 10-K metrics show the trade-off between breadth and depth: in 2024 Evolent averaged about 7.0 million Performance Suite lives at about $21.44 PMPM, versus 73.3 million Specialty Technology and Services lives at about $0.38 PMPM. Performance Suite growth drove 2024 revenue to $2.55 billion. By Q4 2025, average Performance Suite lives were about 6.5 million and reported PMPM fell sharply after some contracts moved from gross to net revenue accounting, so PMPM trends across years are not directly comparable.

facts.mechanism: fixed PMPM fee; Evolent bears medical cost within a specialty scope

summary: Signify Health runs a national mobile network of credentialed clinicians who visit Medicare Advantage and managed Medicaid members at home to perform in-home health evaluations (IHEs), plus select diagnostic screenings, care-gap closure and social-needs screening. Its customers are mainly health plans, which pay per completed evaluation; in 2021 Humana, Aetna and Optum accounted for about 26%, 24% and 11% of revenue and its top ten customers about 78%. Signify's own filings note that IHE findings can feed the diagnosis data that support plans' risk adjustment scores and HEDIS and Star measures, and that plans could seek repayment if CMS or OIG audits invalidate those diagnoses. Volume has grown steadily: over 1.9 million IHEs in 2021 (1.4 million in 2020) on revenue of $773.4 million; under CVS ownership, more than 3.5 million IHEs in 2025.

summary: In February 2022 Signify Health agreed to buy Caravan Health, a Kansas City company that organized and managed accountable care organizations, especially "collaborative" ACOs that pool smaller health systems and practices, mostly in the Medicare Shared Savings Program. The reported price was about $250 million upfront in cash and Signify stock, with additional contingent payments of up to $50 million reported by some outlets. The combined companies cited more than 3,200 health systems and practices and 10,000 primary care physicians. Caravan founder Lynn Barr became Signify's chief innovation officer. The ACO book later passed to CVS and, in March 2025, CVS divested its MSSP operations to Wellvana Health.

summary: Signify had become the largest convener in CMS's Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced model through its Remedy Partners business, managing $4.62 billion of episode spend in 2021; BPCI-A services were about 14% of Signify revenue that year. In early July 2022 Signify announced it would wind down this Episodes of Care segment and exit BPCI-A, arguing that CMS's retrospective trend adjustment lowered target prices after the fact, could not be forecast, and made the program unsustainable for conveners. Fierce Healthcare reported the wind-down would eliminate nearly 500 jobs. The company said it would refocus on its home-based services and the newly acquired Caravan Health ACO business. The episode is a useful example of how benchmark-setting rules, not just care performance, can determine whether intermediaries can sustain risk in CMS models.

summary: Optum Health is UnitedHealth Group's care delivery and care management business, offering primary, specialty and surgical care, behavioral and complex-care programs, post-acute planning, home and virtual care. UnitedHealth's 10-K describes three payment types: fully accountable value-based arrangements, in which Optum Health takes responsibility for patients' health care costs in exchange for a monthly premium (typically per patient per month) paid by a health plan; administrative fee arrangements; and fee-for-service. It says Optum Health serves more than 100 payer partners, so its risk contracts extend beyond UnitedHealthcare, although the filing does not break out the share tied to its sister insurer. Under accounting rules these risk contracts are booked as premium revenue, and when expected costs exceed future premiums Optum must record a loss contract reserve, which it did for 2026 in late 2025.

summary: Humana treats provider risk contracts as central to its integrated care strategy. At December 31, 2025 about 2,260,900 members, or 15.1% of its total medical membership, were covered under shared-risk value-based arrangements covering all member benefits, including 1,947,900 individual Medicare Advantage members, or 37.1% of individual MA membership. Under typical capitation, Humana prepays providers a fixed monthly fee per member covering all or a defined portion of benefits; capitated physicians usually carry stop-loss coverage limiting their annual exposure on any single member. These arrangements may be with independent groups or Humana's own CenterWell clinics. Note that Humana's definition here is limited to full shared-risk arrangements; broader industry counts of "value-based" often include upside-only or pay-for-performance contracts and are not comparable.

facts.mechanism: monthly capitation per member; provider stop-loss

title: Humana–Welsh Carson primary care clinic partnership

summary: Humana built part of its clinic footprint through a strategic partnership with private equity firm Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe (WCAS) to develop senior-focused, payer-agnostic primary care centers off Humana's balance sheet during the start-up years. As of December 31, 2025, 146 clinics were operating under the partnership. The partnership entities reported revenue of about $2.05 billion in 2025 and a net loss of $84 million (2024: $1.99 billion revenue, $92 million loss). The agreements include put and call options, exercisable at a fixed revenue exit multiple with a minimum return to WCAS, under which WCAS can require Humana to buy its interest or Humana can acquire it; at year-end 2025 the put option was valued at about $1.4 billion. This structure shows how new clinics are financed while they mature toward profitability.

title: Cityblock Health: value-based care for Medicaid and dual-eligible members
questions: What does Cityblock Health do?
Who does Cityblock serve?
How is Cityblock different from senior primary care companies?
summary: Cityblock Health, spun out of Alphabet's Sidewalk Labs in 2017 and based in Brooklyn, is a value-based provider for people with complex clinical, behavioral and social needs who are covered by Medicaid or are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid. Instead of opening many senior clinics funded by Medicare Advantage capitation, it partners with Medicaid managed care plans and some health systems to deliver a wrap-around model alongside members' existing primary care: 24/7 access, urgent and primary care extension, behavioral health, social care, clinical pharmacy and care management, with heavy use of community health workers and in-home or community-based outreach. Clinical services are provided by an affiliated professional corporation, Cityblock Medical Practice, P.A., with Cityblock Health supplying management services. EmblemHealth in New York was its first payer partner.

title: Cityblock severe mental illness program results (company study)
questions: Does Cityblock reduce costs?
What evidence is there for Cityblock's model?
What did the Cityblock NEJM Catalyst study find?
summary: In November 2024 Cityblock publicized a study in NEJM Catalyst, authored by its own behavioral health team, of a program for Washington, D.C. Medicaid members with psychotic disorders or severe substance use disorders who were likely to have avoidable behavioral health use. Of 215 identified members, 123 enrolled. Compared with non-enrolled members, the company reported an 11.5% reduction in total cost of care (described as statistically significant) and a 19.7% reduction in inpatient utilization; 95% of identified food needs were addressed. Because the study was conducted by company staff on a small, non-randomized comparison and the matching method was not described in the release, the results should be read as company-reported evidence rather than independent evaluation.

summary: Lumeris is a privately held value-based care enablement company that partners with health systems, physician groups and payers on primary care performance. Its 2026 press materials describe headquarters in St. Louis with operations, including an innovation hub called Tomorrow Labs, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and more than 1,200 employees. title: Why payers bought primary care: Optum, CenterWell, CVS
questions: Why do insurers buy primary care practices?
How do Optum, CenterWell and Oak Street compare?
What is payer-provider vertical integration in Medicare Advantage?
summary: The three largest payer-owned primary care platforms were assembled to capture Medicare Advantage premium economics. A plan pays an owned or affiliated group a monthly premium per member and the group bears medical cost risk, so savings from fewer admissions, better chronic care and complete diagnosis capture accrue inside the parent; the owned provider can also serve rival insurers' members. UnitedHealth's Optum Health reported 4.7 million people in value-based arrangements at end-2024 and about $105 billion of revenue. Humana's CenterWell operated 350 senior clinics with about 491,100 patients and is paid mostly by Humana's own plans. CVS paid about $8 billion for Signify Health (March 2023) and about $10.6 billion enterprise value for Oak Street Health (May 2023), which had 246 centers in 27 states and about 500,000 patients in 2025. Amazon's One Medical, with Iora, is the non-insurer counterpart.

title: Payer-owned care delivery retrenchment in 2025
questions: Is payer-owned value-based primary care struggling?
What write-downs did Optum and CVS take on care delivery?
Why are insurers pulling back from ACO REACH and MSSP?
summary: In 2025 the payer-owned care delivery strategy hit financial strain. Optum Health swung to an operating loss of $278 million on about $102 billion of revenue, booked a $623 million reserve for expected 2026 losses on value-based contracts, and planned to cut value-based membership about 10% in 2026 and narrow its affiliated physician network. CVS recorded a $5.7 billion goodwill impairment on its Health Care Delivery unit after deciding to slow Oak Street clinic openings and close some clinics in 2026, and it exited ACO REACH and sold its MSSP book to Wellvana. Evolent sold its MSSP ACO business to Privia. Filings cite Medicare Advantage funding cuts including risk-model revisions, elevated utilization and medical cost trend, and the acuity of newly added patients. Humana's WCAS clinic partnership also continued to post losses. Enablers focused on MSSP (Privia, Wellvana) were the buyers of these books.

title: Specialty VBC enablement (Evolent) vs primary-care enablement
questions: How is specialty value-based care different from primary care value-based care?
Who is the customer in specialty benefit management?
Why did Evolent leave primary care ACOs?
summary: Primary-care enablement (Optum's affiliated networks, CenterWell's MSO, Lumeris, Privia, Evolent's former ECP) organizes physicians to take total-cost-of-care risk, typically through MSSP, ACO REACH or Medicare Advantage capitation, and earns a share of savings or a capitation margin; the primary care physician is the lever. Specialty enablement, Evolent's current focus, sells to health plans instead: the plan carves out a high-cost domain such as oncology, cardiology or musculoskeletal care and pays a fixed PMPM to a specialist manager that controls cost through evidence-based pathways, prior authorization and provider engagement. Evolent's numbers show the shape: tens of millions of lives at under 40 cents PMPM for administrative specialty services, versus about 7 million lives at roughly $21 PMPM where it bears the specialty cost (2024). Evolent sold its ACO business in 2025 to concentrate on that specialty model.

title: In-home health risk assessment economics and OIG scrutiny
questions: Why do Medicare Advantage plans pay for in-home health assessments?
What did OIG find about health risk assessments?
Are in-home HRAs used to increase risk scores?
How much MA payment comes from HRA-only diagnoses?
summary: Medicare Advantage plans are paid more for members with documented chronic conditions, so a home visit that records diagnoses can raise risk-adjusted payments, alongside care-gap closure and Star-rating benefits. Signify Health's own 10-K acknowledged that its evaluations support plans' risk scores and that audits could lead plans to seek repayment. In October 2024 the HHS Office of Inspector General estimated that diagnoses reported only on HRAs and HRA-linked chart reviews, with no other record of care in 2022, generated about $7.5 billion in 2023 MA payments for 1.7 million enrollees; in-home HRAs and related chart reviews produced almost two-thirds of that, and 20 MA companies accounted for 80%. OIG recommended limiting the use of HRA-only diagnoses and auditing them; CMS agreed only to study which conditions are susceptible. Demand nonetheless grew: CVS reported more than 3.5 million Signify IHEs in 2025.

facts.cms_response: concurred only with recommendation to identify susceptible condition categories
